question: Although the new Lula government has brought with it significant changes with regard to indigenous peoples in Brazil, there are still elements of concern relating to the guarantee of the territories and the protection of the lives of indigenous peoples in the country. Recently, violent attacks against communities in various states of the country have resulted in fatalities.

The killing of Nega, the leader of the indigenous peoples known as the Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe in southern Bahía, is an example of the country's pattern of persistent brutality at the hands of big landowners and owners of large estates, and the accompanying inaction or involvement therein of police forces. In 2023, little progress was made in the demarcation of indigenous lands and only eight territories were approved.

Meanwhile, the Brazilian Congress, acting against a decision of the Supreme Court, recently adopted Law 14.701/23, which imposes a cut-off date in the demarcation policy and opens indigenous lands up to the economic interests of third parties, in violation of the peoples’ constitutional rights.

The EU-Mercosur Agreement could aggravate this situation, as it increases the pressure on these territories from major economic interests. Does the Commission believe that Law 14.701/23 may be at odds with the clauses recently added to the EU-Mercosur Agreement?
answer: The Commission is closely following developments on the ‘Marco Temporal’ bill. Brazil’s Supreme Court has been asked to rule on the constitutionality of the measure. Market opening for agricultural products will be very limited under the EU-Mercosur agreement compared to the overall Brazilian exports.

Furthermore, products exported to the EU will need to comply with EU legislation such as that on deforestation-free supply chains (1) which provides for a platform for engagement with Brazilian business regarding harmful practices in the fields of agro-business and deforestation. Brazil has also demonstrated that it can increase production by improving productivity rather than expanding agricultural areas.

For instance, in the period 2005-2012, Brazilian agricultural production increased, while deforestation and pressure on indigenous territories decreased significantly. Thus, the agreement is not expected to generate additional pressure on indigenous territories. Forest and indigenous protection policies play a key role in mitigating deforestation and pressure on indigenous territories.

The draft agreement with Mercosur already includes clear commitments to respect human rights. The Mercosur agreement has the potential to provide important benefits in that respect, and language on the protection of territories of indigenous people is under discussion in a draft additional legal instrument.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010, OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206-247.
